claim: Cholinergic interneurons (CINs) of the striatum are crucial for normal motor and behavioral functions of the basal ganglia.
source: The cholinergic interneurons (CINs) of the striatum are crucial for normal motor and behavioral functions of the basal ganglia.
evidence: This is a general statement about CIN function that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Striatal CINs exhibit tonic firing punctuated by distinct pauses.
source: Striatal CINs exhibit tonic firing punctuated by distinct pauses.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to prior literature and is consistent with established knowledge about CIN firing patterns.

claim: Pauses in CIN firing occur in response to motivationally significant events.
source: Pauses occur in response to motivationally significant events, but their function is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field about CIN responses to behavioral stimuli.

claim: The function of pauses in CIN firing was unknown prior to this study.
source: Pauses occur in response to motivationally significant events, but their function is unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Optogenetically-induced pauses in CIN firing inhibited subthreshold membrane potential activity of SPNs.
source: We found that optogenetically-induced pauses in CIN firing inhibited subthreshold membrane potential activity and decreased firing of SPNs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from whole cell recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Optogenetically-induced pauses in CIN firing decreased firing of SPNs.
source: We found that optogenetically-induced pauses in CIN firing inhibited subthreshold membrane potential activity and decreased firing of SPNs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from juxtacellular recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: During pauses in CIN firing, SPN membrane potential fluctuations became more hyperpolarized.
source: During pauses, SPN membrane potential fluctuations became more hyperpolarized and UP state durations became shorter.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data from in vivo whole cell recordings shown in Figure 2.

claim: During pauses in CIN firing, UP state durations in SPNs became shorter.
source: During pauses, SPN membrane potential fluctuations became more hyperpolarized and UP state durations became shorter.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data from in vivo whole cell recordings shown in Figure 2.

claim: Short-term plasticity of corticostriatal inputs was decreased during pauses in CIN firing.
source: In addition, short-term plasticity of corticostriatal inputs was decreased during pauses.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data from cortical stimulation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The net effect of the pause in CIN firing on SPNs activity is inhibition in vivo.
source: Our results indicate that, in vivo, the net effect of the pause in CIN firing on SPNs activity is inhibition and provide a novel mechanism for cholinergic control of striatal output.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Acetylcholine is present in high concentrations in the striatum of the basal ganglia.
source: Acetylcholine – the first neurotransmitter to be identified – is present in high concentrations in the striatum of the basal ganglia (Zhou et al., 2001)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2001.

claim: Acetylcholine in the striatum is released by a population of intrinsic cholinergic interneurons that are distinct from the cholinergic projection neurons that innervate the cortex.
source: Acetylcholine – the first neurotransmitter to be identified – is present in high concentrations in the striatum of the basal ganglia (Zhou et al., 2001) where it is released by a population of intrinsic cholinergic interneurons (CINs) that are distinct from the cholinergic projection neurons that innervate the cortex (Woolf and Butcher, 1981).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Woolf and Butcher, 1981.

claim: Recent studies indicate an external cholinergic innervation from the pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental nuclei to the dorsal striatum and nucleus accumbens.
source: In addition, recent studies indicate an external cholinergic innervation from the pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental nuclei to the dorsal striatum and nucleus accumbens (Dautan et al., 2016, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dautan et al., 2016, 2014.

claim: CINs play an important role in behavior by modulating the activity of spiny projection neurons (SPNs).
source: CINs play an important role in behavior by modulating the activity of the principal output neurons of the striatum, the spiny projection neurons (SPNs) (Witten et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Witten et al., 2010.

claim: There has been great interest in the role of CINs in disorders of the basal ganglia.
source: Previously there has been great interest in the role of CINs in disorders of the basal ganglia (Maurice et al., 2015; Pisani et al., 2007; Shen et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Maurice et al., 2015; Pisani et al., 2007; Shen et al., 2015.

claim: There has been recent interest in the role of CINs in behavioral flexibility.
source: Previously there has been great interest in the role of CINs in disorders of the basal ganglia (Maurice et al., 2015; Pisani et al., 2007; Shen et al., 2015) and more recently in behavioral flexibility (Aoki et al., 2015; Bradfield et al., 2013; Okada et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Aoki et al., 2015; Bradfield et al., 2013; Okada et al., 2014.

claim: CINs are tonically active.
source: CINs are tonically active (Wilson et al., 1990)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 1990.

claim: CINs represent only 1% of striatal neurons.
source: CINs are tonically active (Wilson et al., 1990) and although they represent only 1% of striatal neurons their extensive axonal fields allow them to control large striatal regions (Bolam et al., 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the proportion of CINs in the striatum.

claim: CINs have extensive axonal fields that allow them to control large striatal regions.
source: CINs are tonically active (Wilson et al., 1990) and although they represent only 1% of striatal neurons their extensive axonal fields allow them to control large striatal regions (Bolam et al., 1984).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bolam et al., 1984.

claim: CINs have a diverse array of receptors for acetylcholine at both pre- and post-synaptic locations.
source: These features combine with a diverse array of receptors for acetylcholine both at pre- and post-synaptic locations (Hernández-Echeagaray et al., 1998; Hersch et al., 1994; Sugita et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hernández-Echeagaray et al., 1998; Hersch et al., 1994; Sugita et al., 1991.

claim: CINs are crucial modulators of striatal function.
source: Thus, CINs are crucial modulators of striatal function.
evidence: This is inferred from the preceding statements about CIN properties and their effects on striatal circuits.

claim: CINs control SPN excitability and response to glutamatergic inputs via activation of postsynaptic muscarinic type 1 receptors (M1).
source: In particular, CINs control SPN excitability and response to glutamatergic inputs via activation of postsynaptic muscarinic type 1 receptors (M1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cholinergic modulation of SPNs.

claim: CINs exert a tonic inhibitory influence over incoming information via the activation of muscarinic type 2 (M2/M4) receptors located on cortical and thalamic glutamatergic terminals.
source: At the presynaptic level CINs exert a tonic inhibitory influence over incoming information via the activation of muscarinic type 2 (M2/M4) receptors located on cortical and thalamic glutamatergic terminals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about presynaptic cholinergic modulation.

claim: The firing pattern of CINs in vivo varies according to behavioural context.
source: The firing pattern of CINs in vivo varies according to behavioural context.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CIN firing patterns in different behavioral states.

claim: During slow wave activity or activated brain states, spontaneous CIN activity ranges from tonic firing to bursts of firing separated by pauses of variable duration.
source: During slow wave activity or activated brain states, spontaneous CIN activity ranges from tonic firing, which may be regular or irregular, to bursts of firing separated by pauses of variable duration (Sharott et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sharott et al., 2012.

claim: In awake animals exposed to repeated, motivationally significant stimuli, putative CINs respond by a pause in firing.
source: In awake animals exposed to repeated, motivationally significant stimuli, putative CINs respond by a pause in firing (Graybiel et al., 1994; Kimura et al., 1984; Morris et al., 2004), sometimes preceded and often followed by a burst.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Graybiel et al., 1994; Kimura et al., 1984; Morris et al., 2004.

claim: CIN pauses in response to motivationally significant stimuli are sometimes preceded and often followed by a burst.
source: In awake animals exposed to repeated, motivationally significant stimuli, putative CINs respond by a pause in firing (Graybiel et al., 1994; Kimura et al., 1984; Morris et al., 2004), sometimes preceded and often followed by a burst.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Graybiel et al., 1994; Kimura et al., 1984; Morris et al., 2004.

claim: Previous work has focused on the effects of the burst component of CIN firing.
source: Previous work (Crittenden et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2010; Doig et al., 2014; English et al., 2011; Nelson et al., 2014) has focused on the effects of the burst component.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Crittenden et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2010; Doig et al., 2014; English et al., 2011; Nelson et al., 2014.

claim: In awake animals, the pause in CIN firing has been reported to have either no reliable effects with pauses of short duration or a mixture of excitation and inhibition during pauses of long duration on firing activity of SPNs recorded extracellularly.
source: In awake animals, the pause has been reported to have either no reliable effects with pauses of short duration (English et al., 2011), or a mixture of excitation and inhibition during pauses of long duration (Witten et al., 2010) on firing activity of SPNs recorded extracellularly.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to English et al., 2011 and Witten et al., 2010.

claim: This study focuses on the effects of the pause on subthreshold membrane potential fluctuations of SPNs recorded intracellularly.
source: Here we focus on the effects of the pause on subthreshold membrane potential fluctuations of SPNs recorded intracellularly, as well as supratheshold firing activity of SPNs identified by juxtacellular recording in vivo.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach of the current study.

claim: This study used optogenetic silencing of CINs optimized to produce a pause in nearby CINs during whole-cell and juxtacellular electrophysiological recording from CINs and SPNs in vivo.
source: We used optogenetic silencing of CINs – optimized to produce a pause in nearby CINs – during whole-cell and juxtacellular electrophysiological recording from CINs and SPNs in vivo.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: A pause in CIN firing caused an inhibitory effect on SPN activity in vivo, reversing expectations based on in vitro studies and computational theories.
source: We found that a pause in CIN firing caused an inhibitory effect on SPN activity in vivo, reversing expectations based on in vitro studies and computational theories (Ashby and Crossley, 2011; Franklin and Frank, 2015; Pakhotin and Bracci, 2007)
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data, and contrasts with prior expectations from cited literature.

claim: The findings complement previous in vivo findings.
source: We found that a pause in CIN firing caused an inhibitory effect on SPN activity in vivo, reversing expectations based on in vitro studies and computational theories (Ashby and Crossley, 2011; Franklin and Frank, 2015; Pakhotin and Bracci, 2007) and complementing previous in vivo findings (English et al., 2011; Witten et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement relates the current findings to previous in vivo studies cited.

claim: A pause in CIN firing hyperpolarizes the membrane potential of SPNs in vivo.
source: In particular, a pause in CIN firing hyperpolarizes the membrane potential of SPNs and reduces the short-term plasticity at cortical inputs, leading to decreased firing of SPNs in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from whole cell recordings.

claim: A pause in CIN firing reduces the short-term plasticity at cortical inputs to SPNs.
source: In particular, a pause in CIN firing hyperpolarizes the membrane potential of SPNs and reduces the short-term plasticity at cortical inputs, leading to decreased firing of SPNs in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from cortical stimulation experiments.

claim: An adeno-associated virus (AAV) encoding the neuronal silencer Halorhodopsin (NpHR) was injected into the striatum of ChAT-cre mice to induce pauses in CINs that mimic naturally occurring pauses.
source: We injected an adeno-associated virus (AAV) encoding the neuronal silencer Halorhodopsin (NpHR) into the striatum of ChAT-cre mice to induce pauses in CINs that mimic naturally occurring pauses (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Histological analysis confirmed that the expression of NpHR was restricted to CINs in the dorsal striatum.
source: Histological analysis confirmed that the expression of NpHR was restricted to CINs in the dorsal striatum (Figure 1B and Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: 99.0 ± 0.48% of the cells that expressed NpHR-eYFP also stained for anti-ChAT.
source: We found that the 99.0 ± 0.48% of the cells that expressed NpHR-eYFP also stained for anti-ChAT leaving only 1.0 ± 0.48% that were non-specifically expressing NpHR-eYFP.
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunohistochemical analysis demonstrating specificity of viral transduction.

claim: Only 1.0 ± 0.48% of cells expressing NpHR-eYFP were non-specifically expressing NpHR-eYFP (not ChAT positive).
source: We found that the 99.0 ± 0.48% of the cells that expressed NpHR-eYFP also stained for anti-ChAT leaving only 1.0 ± 0.48% that were non-specifically expressing NpHR-eYFP.
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunohistochemical analysis demonstrating specificity of viral transduction.

claim: Injections targeting the dorsal striatum infected 57.35 ± 4.33% of ChAT positive neurons.
source: Our injections targeting the dorsal striatum infected 57.35 ± 4.33% of ChAT positive neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Whole cell recordings obtained both in acute slices and in vivo from anaesthetized mice showed that a brief pulse of light produced a hyperpolarization of the membrane potential of CINs, causing a pause of their tonic firing.
source: Whole cell recordings obtained both in acute slices and in vivo from anaesthetized mice showed that a brief pulse of light produced a hyperpolarization of the membrane potential of CINs, causing a pause of their tonic firing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from whole cell recordings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In all CINs tested, NpHR-induced inhibition caused complete silencing of firing during light.
source: The average peristimulus time histogram (PSTH) shows that in all CINs tested, NpHR-induced inhibition caused complete silencing of firing during light (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is experimental data from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Optically identified CINs were separated from putative SPNs based on their distinct firing properties and spike waveforms.
source: Optically identified CINs were separated from putative SPNs based on their distinct firing properties and spike waveforms (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplements 2—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the methodology for cell type identification, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A light pulse of 0.5 or 1 s induced a complete pause of ongoing firing in all CINs.
source: To differentiate optogenetically induced pauses from those occurring during the resetting of autonomous activity (interspike interval ranging from 138 to 902 ms) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplements 2—source data 1.), we delivered a light pulse of 0.5 or 1 s which induced a complete pause of ongoing firing in all CINs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and Figure 1G).
evidence: This is experimental data from juxtacellular recordings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and Figure 1G.

claim: The pause in CIN firing was followed by rebound firing with a variable onset (0.5 s: 105.6 ± 11.2 ms, n = 16; 1 s: 69.37 ± 8.8 ms, n = 16).
source: The pause was followed by rebound firing with a variable onset (0.5 s: 105.6 ± 11.2 ms, n = 16; 1 s: 69.37 ± 8.8 ms, n = 16) and stayed two standard deviations (S.D.) above the mean for 79.3 ± 12.6 ms (0.5 s pause) and 138.12 ± 14.6 ms (1 s pause) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and Figure 1G).
evidence: This is quantitative data from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and Figure 1G.

claim: Rebound firing after the pause stayed two standard deviations above the mean for 79.3 ± 12.6 ms (0.5 s pause) and 138.12 ± 14.6 ms (1 s pause).
source: The pause was followed by rebound firing with a variable onset (0.5 s: 105.6 ± 11.2 ms, n = 16; 1 s: 69.37 ± 8.8 ms, n = 16) and stayed two standard deviations (S.D.) above the mean for 79.3 ± 12.6 ms (0.5 s pause) and 138.12 ± 14.6 ms (1 s pause) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and Figure 1G).
evidence: This is quantitative data from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and Figure 1G.

claim: The light-induced pause in CIN firing caused inhibition of firing activity in SPNs.
source: The light-induced pause in CIN firing caused inhibition of firing activity in SPNs (Figure 1I and Figure 1J) which dropped below 2 s.D. from the mean firing frequency (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is experimental data from juxtacellular recordings shown in Figures 1I, 1J, and 1K.

claim: In response to a 1 s exposure to light, the group average (n = 22 cells) PSTH showed a significant decrease in firing rate commencing at the 400–500 ms bin at the p<0.01 level.
source: In response to a 1 s exposure to light, the group average (n = 22 cells) PSTH showed a significant decrease in firing rate commencing at the 400–500 ms bin (red bins, Figure 1K) at the p<0.01 level (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: When individual cells were analyzed, within the group of cells exposed to 1 s light, a total of 14/22 cells showed a significant (p<0.05) decrease in firing, at a median latency of 700 ms from the light pulse.
source: When individual cells were analyzed, within the group of cells exposed to 1 s light, a total of 14/22 cells showed a significant (p<0.05) decrease in firing, at a median latency of 700 ms from the light pulse.
evidence: This is statistical analysis of individual cell responses from experimental data.

claim: Three cells showed a significant (p<0.05) increase in firing after the light pulse.
source: Three cells showed a significant (p<0.05) increase in firing after the light pulse, one cell showed a significant increase (p<0.05) followed by a significant decrease (p<0.05), and four cells showed no significant change in firing rate.
evidence: This is statistical analysis of individual cell responses from experimental data.

claim: One cell showed a significant increase (p<0.05) followed by a significant decrease (p<0.05) in firing.
source: Three cells showed a significant (p<0.05) increase in firing after the light pulse, one cell showed a significant increase (p<0.05) followed by a significant decrease (p<0.05), and four cells showed no significant change in firing rate.
evidence: This is statistical analysis of individual cell responses from experimental data.

claim: Four cells showed no significant change in firing rate in response to the light pulse.
source: Three cells showed a significant (p<0.05) increase in firing after the light pulse, one cell showed a significant increase (p<0.05) followed by a significant decrease (p<0.05), and four cells showed no significant change in firing rate.
evidence: This is statistical analysis of individual cell responses from experimental data.

claim: A total of 9/14 of the cells showing an inhibitory response (64%) showed a significant (p<0.05) decrease within the 1 s light on period, median latency of 400 msec.
source: To determine which responses were due to the pause (and not the rebound firing activity), we tested cells for inhibition during the light on period. A total of 9/14 of the cells showing an inhibitory response (64%) showed a significant (p<0.05) decrease within the 1 s light on period, median latency of 400 msec.
evidence: This is statistical analysis of individual cell responses from experimental data.

claim: Light-induced pauses of CINs resulted in a similar inhibition of SPNs firing both in anesthetized mice (1 s: 43.7 ± 6.32 % n=22) and in awake, head restrained mice (51.52 ± 13.9 % n=7).
source: Light-induced pauses of CINs resulted in a similar inhibition of SPNs firing both in anesthetized mice (1 s: 43.7 ± 6.32 % n=22) and in awake, head restrained mice (51.52 ± 13.9 % n=7) (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is quantitative data from juxtacellular recordings in both anesthetized and awake mice shown in Figure 1L.

claim: A pause in CIN firing of 1 s duration significantly reduces the firing of SPNs in vivo.
source: These results indicate that a pause in CIN firing of 1 s duration significantly reduces the firing of SPNs in vivo.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data on SPN firing during CIN pauses.

claim: In the cells exposed to a 0.5 s light on period (n = 17 cells), the group average PSTH showed a significant decrease in firing rate at the 400–500 ms bin.
source: In the cells exposed to a 0.5 s light on period (n = 17 cells), the group average PSTH showed a significant decrease in firing rate at the 400–500 ms bin (red bins, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: When individual cells were analyzed, none of the cells (0/17) showed a significant decrease during the 0.5 s period of light on.
source: When individual cells were analyzed, however, none of the cells (0/17) showed a significant decrease during the 0.5 s period of light on.
evidence: This is statistical analysis of individual cell responses from experimental data.

claim: A pause in CIN firing of 0.5 s duration was not of sufficient duration for the effect that was observed reliably with 1 s duration.
source: These results indicate that a pause in CIN firing of 0.5 s duration was not of sufficient duration for the effect that was observed reliably with 1 s duration.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing the effects of 0.5 s versus 1 s pauses on SPN firing.

claim: There was no significant increase in SPN firing from the baseline at the end of the light on period until 700–800 ms after the light off (p<0.01).
source: To determine the effect of the transition from light on to light offset, we analyzed the activity of SPNs in the period after the light offset, relative to the last 500 ms of the light on period. There was no significant increase from this new baseline until 700–800 ms after the light off (p<0.01, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of experimental data examining the recovery period after the pause.

claim: The firing rate remained more than 2 s.D. below the initial baseline mean after the light offset.
source: Consistent with this, the firing rate remained more than 2 s.D. below the initial baseline mean (magenta bins, Figure 1K).
evidence: This is analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Under ketamine/xylazine anesthesia, SPNs showed a characteristic bimodal distribution of the membrane potential, fluctuating between a DOWN state and an UP state.
source: Under these conditions SPNs showed a characteristic bimodal distribution of the membrane potential, fluctuating between a DOWN state, characterized by hyperpolarized potentials, and an UP state, where the cell is close to threshold for firing (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is experimental observation from in vivo whole cell recordings shown in Figure 2B.

claim: During a pause (5 s) in CIN firing, the membrane potential of SPNs shifts to more hyperpolarized values in the DOWN state (before: −71.59 ± 1.82 mV; pause: −72.77 ± 1.86 mV; after: −71.66 ± 1.75 mV; n = 13).
source: The best-fit of the sum of two Gaussian distributions to the all-amplitudes distribution of the membrane potential revealed that, during a pause (5 s) in CIN firing, the membrane potential of SPNs shifts to more hyperpolarized values in the DOWN state (before: −71.59 ± 1.82 mV; pause: −72.77 ± 1.86 mV; after: −71.66 ± 1.75 mV; n = 13; Repeated Measure One-way ANOVA, F(2, 24)=7.692; p=0.0026; Figure 2C and Figure 2D).
evidence: This is quantitative data from in vivo whole cell recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: The UP state potential was significantly more hyperpolarized during a pause (before: −56.35 ± 1.85 mV; pause: −57.79 ± 2.01 mV; after: −55.89 ± 1.83 mV; n = 13).
source: The UP state potential was also significantly more hyperpolarized during a pause (before: −56.35 ± 1.85 mV; pause: −57.79 ± 2.01 mV; after: −55.89 ± 1.83 mV; n = 13; Repeated Measure One-way ANOVA, F(2, 24)=6.139; p = 0.0070 Figure 2C and Figure 2D).
evidence: This is quantitative data from in vivo whole cell recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: A decrease in the number of points during the UP state was observed, suggesting a shortened duration.
source: We also observed a decrease in the number of points during the UP state, thus suggesting a shortened duration (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 2C, with an inference about UP state duration.

claim: UP states were significantly shorter during a pause (before: 0.42 ± 0.02 s; pause: 0.39 ± 0.01 s; after: 0.41 ± 0.02 s; n = 13).
source: We observed significantly shorter UP states during a pause (before: 0.42 ± 0.02 s; pause: 0.39 ± 0.01 s; after: 0.41 ± 0.02 s; n = 13; Repeated Measure One-way ANOVA, F(2, 24)=11.56, p=0.0003; Figure 2E)
evidence: This is quantitative data from in vivo whole cell recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: DOWN state durations were significantly increased during a pause (before: 0.51 ± 0.03 s; pause: 0.55 ± 0.04 s; after: 0.5 ± 0.04 s; n = 13).
source: while DOWN state durations were significantly increased (before: 0.51 ± 0.03 s; pause: 0.55 ± 0.04 s; after: 0.5 ± 0.04 s; n = 13; Repeated Measure One-way ANOVA, F(2,24) = 5.874, p=0.0084; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is quantitative data from in vivo whole cell recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The number of action potentials fired in the UP states during a pause was significantly decreased (before: 1.94 ± 0.11 Hz; pause: 0.86 ± 0.08 Hz; after: 1.97 ± 0.13 Hz; n = 334, 319, 325 UP states respectively).
source: The number of action potentials fired in the UP states during a pause was significantly decreased (before: 1.94 ± 0.11 Hz; pause: 0.86 ± 0.08 Hz; after: 1.97 ± 0.13 Hz; n = 334, 319, 325 UP states respectively; One-way ANOVA, F(2, 975)=33.16, p<0.0001; Figure 2F)
evidence: This is quantitative data from in vivo whole cell recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: UP states did not exhibit significant changes in the mean amplitude during a pause (before: 17.23 ± 1.02 mV; pause: 16.34 ± 1.27 mV; after: 16.83 ± 1.12 mV; n = 13).
source: UP states did not exhibit significant changes in the mean amplitude (before: 17.23 ± 1.02 mV; pause: 16.34 ± 1.27 mV; after: 16.83 ± 1.12 mV; n = 13; Repeated Measure One-way ANOVA, F(2, 24)=1.88 p=0.1748; data not shown)
evidence: This is quantitative data from in vivo whole cell recordings with statistical analysis.

claim: UP states did not exhibit significant changes in their frequency during a pause (before: 1.03 ± 0.04 Hz; pause: 0.98 ± 0.05 Hz; after: 1.0 ± 0.05 Hz; n = 13).
source: nor in their frequency (before: 1.03 ± 0.04 Hz; pause: 0.98 ± 0.05 Hz; after: 1.0 ± 0.05 Hz; n = 13; Repeated Measure One-way ANOVA, F(2, 24)=2.039, p=0.1521; data not shown).
evidence: This is quantitative data from in vivo whole cell recordings with statistical analysis.

claim: The transition from DOWN to UP state was significantly slower during a pause (before: 145.9 ± 17.52 mV/s; pause: 127.7 ± 16.87 mV/s; after: 139 ± 17.76 mV/s; n = 13).
source: However, the transition from DOWN to UP state was significantly slower during a pause (before: 145.9 ± 17.52 mV/s; pause: 127.7 ± 16.87 mV/s; after: 139 ± 17.76 mV/s; n = 13; Repeated Measure One-way ANOVA, F(2, 24)=5.09, p=0.0144; Figure 2G and Figure 2H).
evidence: This is quantitative data from in vivo whole cell recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figures 2G and 2H.

claim: A pause in CIN firing decreases the excitability of SPNs in vivo.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that a pause in CIN firing decreases the excitability of SPNs in vivo.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data on membrane potential fluctuations and firing during pauses.

claim: The altered DOWN and UP state dynamics could not be due to a change in the activity of extrinsic afferents because the optogenetic stimulation and expression of NpHR is virtually specific to the striatal CINs.
source: The altered DOWN and UP state dynamics we observed could not be due a change in the activity of extrinsic afferents because the optogenetic stimulation and expression of NpHR is virtually specific to the striatal CINs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity of the optogenetic manipulation demonstrated earlier in the manuscript.

claim: UP states in the anesthetized animal represent the synchronous activation of cortical inputs.
source: Because UP states in the anesthetized animal represent the synchronous activation of cortical inputs we investigated if a pause in CIN firing affected the responsiveness of SPNs to repetitive synaptic inputs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the nature of UP states under anesthesia.

claim: In control conditions (before a pause in CIN firing), a train of 10 stimuli at 25 Hz induced a gradual facilitation and summation of EPSPs over the course of the train.
source: In control conditions (before a pause in CIN firing), a train of 10 stimuli at 25 Hz, induced a gradual facilitation and summation of EPSPs over the course of the train (Figure 3B and Figure 3C).
evidence: This is experimental data from cortical stimulation experiments shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: During the pause in CIN firing, there was a significant increase in the amplitude of the first EPSP in the stimulus train (before: 4.3 ± 0.65 mV; pause: 5.16 ± 0.67 mV; n = 9; paired t-test, p=0.0115).
source: During the pause in CIN firing, we also observed a significant increase in the amplitude of the first EPSP in the stimulus train (before: 4.3 ± 0.65 mV; pause: 5.16 ± 0.67 mV; n = 9; paired t-test, p=0.0115; Figure 3B and Figure 3D).
evidence: This is quantitative data from cortical stimulation experiments with statistical analysis shown in Figures 3B and 3D.

claim: A pause in CIN firing gates cortical information transfer at striatal synapses in vivo.

source: In agreement with previous observations (Maurice et al., 2015) the light-induced pause produced a significant increase in rheobase current compared to control or after light (control: 310 ± 22.09; light: 333.3 ± 20.94; after: 313.3 ± 21.08; n = 12; Repeated Measure One-way ANOVA, F(2, 22)=33.79, p<0.0001; Figure 4B)

source: In agreement with previous observations (Maurice et al., 2015) the light-induced pause produced a significant increase in rheobase current compared to control or after light (control: 310 ± 22.09; light: 333.3 ± 20.94; after: 313.3 ± 21.08; n = 12; Repeated Measure One-way ANOVA, F(2, 22)=33.79, p<0.0001; Figure 4B), and a significant decrease in the number of action potentials fired in response to a current pulse (n = 12; two-way ANOVA, current x light interaction, F(16, 176)=1.77, p=0.039; Figure 4C).

claim: A pause in CIN firing decreased intrinsic excitability of SPNs.
source: Thus, we confirmed that a pause in CIN firing decreased intrinsic excitability of SPNs.

source: We found that, similar to the effect of a pause, bath application of low concentrations of M1 receptor antagonist pirenzepine (100 nM), increased the rheobase current (control: 280 ± 32.66; light: 308.6 ± 32.32; pirenzepine: 302.9 ± 30.99; pirenzepine and light: 305.7 ± 34.01; n = 7; Repeated Measure One-way ANOVA, F(3, 18)=16.37, p<0.0001; Figure 4E)

source: We found that, similar to the effect of a pause, bath application of low concentrations of M1 receptor antagonist pirenzepine (100 nM), increased the rheobase current (control: 280 ± 32.66; light: 308.6 ± 32.32; pirenzepine: 302.9 ± 30.99; pirenzepine and light: 305.7 ± 34.01; n = 7; Repeated Measure One-way ANOVA, F(3, 18)=16.37, p<0.0001; Figure 4E) and significantly shifted the relationship between current injection and number of action potential to the right (n = 7; two-way ANOVA, current x light interaction, F(24, 144)=2.519, p=0.0004; Figure 4F).

claim: The M1 receptor antagonist occluded the effect of the light, in that the combined effect of pirenzepine and light on the intrinsic excitability of SPNs was not significantly different from the individual effects.

source: These results suggest that interruption of M1 receptor activation during a pause is sufficient to decrease SPN excitability (Figure 4G).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the pirenzepine occlusion experiments.

evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings from the study.

claim: Pauses in CIN firing caused a significant decrease in the firing rate of SPNs measured using in vivo juxtacellular recordings.
source: Pauses in CIN firing caused hyperpolarization of subthreshold membrane potential fluctuations measured by in vivo whole-cell recording and caused a significant decrease in the firing rate of SPNs measured using in vivo juxtacellular recordings.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from the study.

claim: During a pause there was a slower transition between hyperpolarized and depolarized membrane potentials.

evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from the study.

First, our data show a pause mediated inhibition caused by interruption of cholinergic excitation of SPNs. Second, English et al. source: In anaesthetized animals pauses of duration 380–800 ms have been reported in response to a light stimulus (Schulz et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schulz et al., 2011.

source: In vivo, spontaneous firing activity is broken up by pauses that vary in duration up to one second (Sharott et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sharott et al., 2012.

(2011), while longer pauses may engage a dual mechanism involving pause-related removal of muscarinic excitation via M1 receptors, in addition to GABA inhibition activated on the rebound.

source: We used NpHR to optogenetically silence CINs during 0.5 and 1 s pauses for recording responses of SPNs in juxtacellular configuration, and changes in membrane potential fluctuations in cells recorded in whole-cell mode during 5 s pauses.
